idiomatic.rationale: Reads like current Angular 22 documentation: standalone signal components, resolver+input binding, SSR server routes, transfer state, new core decorators. The only deviations are a redundant hydration feature flag and global stylesheets — nits, not framework-fighting; the custom /_data transport is a documented, well-bounded alternative to HttpClient.

The gaps are failure-mode handling for API errors and two caches that are bounded poorly (by nothing, and by count rather than bytes).

review_cost.rationale: Approve after a small round: one error-handling provider, a cache-eviction line, and a few dependency/config nits. No structural rework.

findings.issue: No withNavigationErrorHandler and no resolver error fallback: when /_data or the API fails (non-404), the resolver rejects, navigation is silently blocked and the user stays on a stale page with no indication anything went wrong.
findings.suggestion: Add withNavigationErrorHandler (or catchError in the resolver returning a RedirectCommand/fallback VM) and surface a minimal error state; on the server, add an Express error handler that returns a branded 500 without a stack trace.

findings.issue: SSR render failures fall through to Express's default error handler, which prints stack traces to the client when NODE_ENV is not 'production' (nothing in the repo sets it).
findings.suggestion: Add an explicit express error-handler middleware that logs server-side and responds with a clean 500, and document setting NODE_ENV=production for npm start.

findings.issue: The module-level client cache is unbounded: entries are only removed on rejection or lazily skipped on TTL expiry, so a long-lived session accumulates every visited page's view model.
findings.suggestion: Cap the Map size (delete-oldest on insert, mirroring the eviction in api-client.ts) or sweep expired entries on write.

findings.issue: Server cache is capped at 4000 entries but is byte-blind; full PokeAPI documents can be 100-300 KB each, so worst-case memory approaches hundreds of MB.
findings.suggestion: Reduce MAX_ENTRIES or add a rough byte budget alongside the entry-count cap.

findings.issue: allowedHosts: ['*'] deviates from the official SSR guidance to keep an explicit host list; the in-code justification is plausible but a reviewer should confirm the reverse-proxy assumption holds in production.
findings.suggestion: Keep an explicit host list if the production proxy host is known, or link the deviation to the deployment doc so the assumption is reviewed with the app.

findings.issue: provideClientHydration(withEventReplay()) is redundant on Angular 22: incremental hydration (enabled by default) already includes event replay.
@angular/forms is declared as a dependency but never imported (no ngModel/FormsModule usage anywhere in src/).
All component styling lives in one ~570-line global stylesheet; classes such as .count and .facts are shared implicitly across components, so collisions and dead rules will accumulate over time.
findings.suggestion: Move page/component-specific blocks (cards, stats, move tables, filters) into the owning components' styles; keep only tokens and layout primitives global.

findings.issue: The linkedSignal + mutable pushedQ coordination for the search box is correct but subtle (URL-driven vs user-typed value), and has no test pinning its edge cases (e.g. back/forward during a pending debounce).
findings.suggestion: Add a small unit test for searchText behaviour across q changes, or extract the 'value that follows a source unless it was just pushed' logic into a named helper with a doc comment.

findings.issue: All six page loaders live in one ~330-line module; fine today, but it will become the file everyone edits as pages grow.
findings.suggestion: Split per page (loaders/pokemon.ts, loaders/home.ts, …) with the shared helpers in a small internal module when the next page type lands.

summary: An exemplary Angular 22 codebase: current idioms everywhere (signal components, resolver+input binding, SSR server routes, @Service, RESPONSE_INIT 404s), a deliberately designed and well-documented server/client VM boundary, and careful spec-driven details like custom scroll policy and missing-value sorting. The real gaps are failure-mode handling — API errors silently strand client-side navigation and surface as bare 500s on first render — plus two sloppily bounded caches and a few config/dependency nits. I'd merge after one small, contained round of changes.
